title: The One Thing You Must Do To Avoid Stress And Improve Behavior improve-behavior/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Michael Linsin presents what he describes as the single most important piece of advice he gives coaching clients: stop trying to convince students to behave. He argues that lectures, pep talks, glaring, cajoling, and searching for the 'perfect words' are not only ineffective but actively communicate to students that their behavior matters more to the teacher than to themselves, shifting leverage in the relationship toward the student. Instead, Linsin advises letting the classroom management plan do the work — calmly enforcing the agreed-upon consequence and walking away, leaving students alone to process responsibility for their own choices. He claims this single change produces a dramatic reduction in stress among the hundreds of teachers he's coached, while also improving classroom energy, rapport, and student maturity over time. The piece closes by tying the strategy to intrinsic, rather than teacher-dependent, student motivation to behave.
points: The single most impactful piece of coaching advice offered is to stop trying to verbally convince students to behave through lectures, pep talks, or persuasion.
Extra verbal engagement over misbehavior signals to students that their behavior matters more to the teacher than to themselves, shifting leverage toward the student.
The alternative is to let the classroom management plan do the work: calmly enforce the agreed-upon consequence and walk away without commentary.
This approach places 100% of responsibility for reflecting on misbehavior onto the student, rather than the teacher doing the emotional labor for them.
The author reports that this single change has produced dramatic stress reduction across hundreds of coached teachers, alongside improved rapport and student maturity.
quotes: Because every one of the hundreds of teachers I’ve given this advice to—through my coaching practice and personal mentoring—has experienced a dramatic decrease in stress.
If not for this strategy, I don’t think I could have become a teacher—or stayed one for long.
It’s to never again try to convince students to behave. It’s to refrain from pulling them aside for lectures, pep-talks, and counseling sessions.
You see, all that extra attention communicates to students just how much their behavior means to you, which effectively shifts the leverage and control in the relationship over to them.
You let your classroom management plan do the heavy lifting for you. You rely on it exclusively. You fulfill your promise to follow it exactly as it’s written.
They’ll develop a strong, intrinsic desire to behave. Naturally and all on their own.
